power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

text.text: Nearly a decade ago, Mollon, Bosten, Peterzell, and Webster (2017) asked what individual differences can teach visual science and what counts as good experimental practice.
text.formatted: Nearly a decade ago, <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Mollon, Bosten, Peterzell, and Webster (2017)</ref> asked what individual differences can teach visual science and what counts as good experimental practice.

text.text: Studies since then have changed both answers.
The study of individual differences is a paradigm, not a technique, with its own objects, standards of evidence, and products.
Long practiced in the shadows by a small group, it should move into the mainstream and integrate with existing paradigms, treating differences among observers as evidence rather than error.

Its central object is the latent factor, which can earn roles from latent mechanism to established mechanism, computational phenotype, heritable phenotype, endophenotype, or factor-targeted marker, each requiring stricter evidence.
Twelve pillars organize what the paradigm buys, including links across domains and levels and tests of whether constructs are unitary.

Several 2017 conclusions need correction, above all the definition of true individual differences as stable, long-term traits, and the 2017 prescriptions (rank statistics, required test-retest reliability, fixed test order, mandatory blocking, blanket correction for multiple comparisons) each trade one error for another.
Because global artifacts produce general factors, tuned factor structure is itself evidence against them.
The long-term goal is a computational atlas of human visual variation: its mechanisms, their sources, and optimal markers for the clinic and for design.
Most experiments manipulate a stimulus, measure a handful of observers, and treat the differences among them as error.

The standard observer of colorimetry and the standard contrast sensitivity function are monuments to this approach. Cronbach (1957) called experimental and correlational psychology "the two disciplines of scientific psychology."
text.formatted: The standard observer of colorimetry and the standard contrast sensitivity function are monuments to this approach. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Cronbach (1957)</ref> called experimental and correlational psychology "the two disciplines of scientific psychology."

text.text: The experimental discipline brings situational variables under control so that causes can be isolated.

The correlational discipline studies what the experimenter has not learned to control, or never can: the variation that nature has already imposed on people through their genes, development, environment, and history.
Cronbach argued that they needed "combined, not parallel, labors," and Wilmer (2008) opened his call for individual differences research in vision with the same passage.
text.formatted: Cronbach argued that they needed <ref type="bibr">"combined, not parallel, labors," and Wilmer (2008)</ref> opened his call for individual differences research in vision with the same passage.

text.text: The core logic is simple.
If two measurements vary together across observers, they probably share a source of variation; if they vary independently, they probably do not.

Measure an observer's sensitivity at many points along a stimulus dimension, such as spatial frequency, wavelength, hue angle, orientation, or temporal frequency, and the pattern of correlations among those points reveals how many independent sources of variation underlie performance and over what range each one operates (Peterzell, 2016; Peterzell & Teller, 1996; Peterzell, Werner, & Kaplan, 1993 , 1995; Wilmer, 2008).

text.text: Information invisible in a group mean becomes visible in the covariance among observers, and the two kinds of information are independent: neither can be recovered from the other (Cronbach, 1957; Mollon, Bosten, Peterzell, & Webster, 2017; Peterzell, Werner, & Kaplan, 1993 , 1995).

text.text: 1.2 Why call it a paradigm?
Mollon et al. (2017) presented individual differences as a resource to be mined with caution, and devoted half their paper to pitfalls.
text.formatted: <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Mollon et al. (2017)</ref> presented individual differences as a resource to be mined with caution, and devoted half their paper to pitfalls.

text.text: That framing undersold the approach.
Several of the 2017 recommendations were not merely debatable but wrong, and they steer researchers toward worse designs and away from analyses that work.
I argue here for a stronger claim: the study of individual differences in vision is a paradigm, not a technique.
It is not a new paradigm.

It has existed for more than a century, but mostly in the shadows of the experimental mainstream, kept alive by a small group of stalwarts who often worked in isolation and published in scattered places (e.g., Billock & Harding, 1996; Bosten, 2022; de-Wit & Wagemans, 2015; Emery & Webster, 2019; Grzeczkowski, Clarke, Francis, Mast, & Herzog, 2017; Luna & Serrano-Pedraza, 2020; Peterzell, 2016; Peterzell & Teller, 1996; Peterzell, Werner, & Kaplan, 1993; Vogel & Awh, 2008; Wilmer, 2008).
text.formatted: It has existed for more than a century, but mostly in the shadows of the experimental mainstream, kept alive by a small group of stalwarts who often worked in isolation and published in scattered places (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Billock & Harding, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Bosten, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">de-Wit & Wagemans, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Emery & Webster, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Grzeczkowski, Clarke, Francis, Mast, & Herzog, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b107">Luna & Serrano-Pedraza, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">Peterzell, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Peterzell & Teller, 1996;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">Peterzell, Werner, & Kaplan, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b211">Vogel & Awh, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b222">Wilmer, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: The word is not new to this literature either.

Thirty years ago, Peterzell and Teller (1996) described "the individual differences paradigm" as one that "uses simple detection data to assess the unadapted, unmasked visual system" and so avoids many of the assumptions on which masking and adaptation depend.
text.formatted: Thirty years ago, <ref type="bibr">Peterzell and Teller (1996)</ref> described "the individual differences paradigm" as one that "uses simple detection data to assess the unadapted, unmasked visual system" and so avoids many of the assumptions on which masking and adaptation depend.

text.text: What is new is the scope of the claim.

I use the word in Kuhn's (1970) narrow sense of a set of shared exemplars: model problems and their accepted solutions, which tell practitioners what counts as an object of study, as evidence, and as a result.
text.formatted: I use the word in <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Kuhn's (1970)</ref> narrow sense of a set of shared exemplars: model problems and their accepted solutions, which tell practitioners what counts as an object of study, as evidence, and as a result.

text.text: The covariance paradigm has its own exemplars, from König and Dieterici's (1886) derivation of cone sensitivities to the factor-analytic recovery of photopigment spectra, spatial channels, and hue mechanisms described below.
text.formatted: The covariance paradigm has its own exemplars, from <ref type="bibr" target="#b95">König and Dieterici's (1886)</ref> derivation of cone sensitivities to the factor-analytic recovery of photopigment spectra, spatial channels, and hue mechanisms described below.

text.text: It has its own central object, the latent factor, its own standards of evidence, and its own products: counts and tuning functions of mechanisms, individual phenotypic profiles, heritability estimates, and efficient, targeted tests.
The paradigm is not meant to replace the study of the average observer.
Experiments establish causes; the covariance paradigm establishes how variation is organized.
The two answer different questions about the same visual system, and each makes the other stronger.

The shift I argue for is therefore the rise of an old paradigm from the margins to the mainstream, and with it a change in how vision science treats variability among observers: from error to be averaged away to evidence about how vision is organized.
Integration with existing paradigms is the point, not a concession.

Nearly every psychophysical experiment tests more than one observer, so nearly every experiment can report the covariance among its observers alongside its means, at no extra cost in data collection if the stimulus dimension is sampled densely enough.
Models of vision can be required to reproduce both the mean function and the pattern of individual differences (Peterzell, in press-a).
text.formatted: Models of vision can be required to reproduce both the mean function and the pattern of individual differences <ref type="bibr">(Peterzell, in press-a)</ref>.

text.text: Physiology and brain imaging can define their units by covariance across people as well as by group averages.
Genetics needs phenotypes, clinical vision science needs targeted tests, and the paradigm supplies both.
In each case it adds a second, independent test of the same theory.

The title of this paper echoes the question Mollon et al. (2017) asked, "what can be learned and what is good experimental practice?", because I give different answers to both halves of that question.

text.text: Far more can be learned than the 2017 paper claimed, and much of what it called good practice is not.

text.text: Thurstone and his students carried the program into what he called visual thinking.

By 1950 he described seven primary visual abilities, perceptual speed, three space factors, two closure factors, and visual memory, which "seem to represent distinct functional unities so that those who excel in one of these factors do not necessarily excel in the others" (Thurstone, 1950, p. 521).

text.text: His students and successors refined the closure and perceptual factors (Botzum, 1951; Mooney, 1954; Pemberton, 1952; Roff, 1952; Street, 1931) and tested whether closure extends to symbolic and verbal material (French & Messick, 1973). text.text: The turning point came with Wilmer (2008), a paper that deserves more than a place in a list.
text.formatted: The turning point came with <ref type="bibr" target="#b222">Wilmer (2008)</ref>, a paper that deserves more than a place in a list.

text.text: It was a primer, but also a program: it defined what the approach is for and what it could achieve.

It built on a literature that had already worked out the logic and taught it intuitively: Peterzell, Werner, and Kaplan (1993, 1995) and Peterzell and Teller (1996) had shown, with plots of individual curves and of correlations against spatial frequency, how the pattern of covariance reveals the number and tuning of channels.

text.text: What Wilmer added was scope and reach.
It explained plainly why differences among observers carry information that group means cannot.
It defined the approach's three pillars, isolating the functional organization, the biology, and the utility of visual functions.
And it showed how each could be pursued with concrete, testable proposals for stereopsis.
It was generous to the small literature that preceded it, describing the line of work above as the most extensive of its kind.
Above all, it was written for experimentalists.
It made the approach legible to vision scientists who had been taught to average differences away, and it spurred a generation of new researchers to take individual differences seriously.

Wilmer and his colleagues then showed what the program could deliver: face recognition as a reliable, heritable, specific ability (Wilmer et al., 2010 (Wilmer et al., , 2012)), two motion mechanisms that predict two phases of smooth pursuit (Wilmer & Nakayama, 2007), and webbased testing that made samples of thousands routine (Germine et al., 2012).

text.text: Several of its own proposals have since been carried out.

Stereoscopic channels have been mapped by factor analysis and shown to be tuned to retinal rather than object-relative spatial frequency (Peterzell, Enongue, et al., 2026; Peterzell, Serrano-Pedraza, et al., 2017; Reynaud & Hess, 2017), and the question it posed as open, whether stereomotion has separate sustained and transient mechanisms, now has an answer (Llamas-Cornejo et al., 2024).

text.text: Much has changed in a decade.

First, factor analysis has recovered tuned structure in domains where it had rarely been applied: the spatial-frequency, temporal-frequency, and orientation tuning of stereoscopic mechanisms, and whether they are tuned to retinal or objectrelative spatial frequency; the spatiotemporal mechanisms revealed by duration thresholds (Luna & Serrano-Pedraza, 2020); hue and motion-direction scaling; cortical color coding; and the chromatic tuning of numerosity adaptation (Section 3.2.1).

Wagemans' and Herzog's groups have built sustained programs on individual differences in Gestalt perceptual organization and visual illusions (Section 3.1.4).

Every factor begins with observed measures: thresholds, matches, scaling responses, evoked-potential amplitudes.
The first requirement is that the measures be reliable as measures of differences between people.
This is not the same as reliability for detecting differences between conditions.

Tasks designed to produce robust effects across conditions often do so by minimizing variation among observers, so a task can be excellent for experiments and poor for individual differences (Hedge, Powell, & Sumner, 2018; Wilmer, 2008).

text.text: A note on terms.

Throughout this paper, factor means a latent source of shared individual variability, however it is estimated, and factor analysis means the family of covariance-based methods used to estimate such sources.

Statisticians rightly distinguish common factor analysis, principal component analysis, independent component analysis, multidimensional scaling, and structural equation models, which rest on different assumptions and can give different answers; a methods section should name the one used.
But the word factor predates them all and belongs to none of them.

Spearman and Thurstone used it for the underlying sources of individual differences that their methods were designed to find, and earlier work in this tradition referred to "statistical 'sources' of individual variability (or factors)" (Peterzell, Kelly, et al., 1996).

text.text: I use it in that broad sense.
A latent factor is a statistical summary of shared variance: a replicable pattern of covariance among measures.
On its own, a factor is a description, not a cause.

Stable covariance can arise from a common cause, from direct interactions among the measured variables, or from shared artifacts, and the factor model alone cannot tell these apart (Borsboom, Mellenbergh, & van Heerden, 2004).

text.text: The converse also needs care: physiologically distinct mechanisms can produce indistinguishable behavior, so the absence of covariance is not always the absence of a mechanism (Billock, 2020).

text.text: The factor's earning criterion is therefore replicability: the same structure in independent samples, preferably with different observers, laboratories, and apparatus.
Achromatic contrast sensitivity is an encouraging case, because a consistent factor structure has appeared across more than six very different datasets (Peterzell, 2024).

text.text: A latent mechanism is a hypothesized process that the visual system carries out: a spatialfrequency channel, a cone photopigment, a sustained or transient temporal mechanism, a hueselective cortical population.
Reading a factor as a mechanism requires evidence beyond covariance, of three main kinds.
The first is theory: the factor's tuning should be interpretable in terms of known or plausible processes.

The second is convergent and discriminant evidence: the factor should appear in different tasks that tap the same process and should separate from factors that tap different processes (Campbell & Fiske, 1959).

text.text: The third, when it is available, is ground truth: a known answer the method should recover.
Ground truth is rare in perception, but it exists.

In mice engineered to express a human long-wavelength photopigment (Jacobs, Williams, Cahill, & Nathans, 2007), factor analysis of spectral sensitivity recovers factors that match the known middle-and long-wavelength opsin spectra (Peterzell, 2026h).

text.text: The same evidence can also show that a factor is not the mechanism it appeared to be.
For decades, factor analyses of contrast sensitivity recovered factors at high spatial frequencies that were read as neural channels.

When contrast sensitivity was measured with and without adaptive-optics correction in the same observers, the factor that dominated sensitivity above about 2 cycles per degree disappeared under correction.
It reflected the optical quality of the eye, not a neural channel (Peterzell & Elliott, 2026).

text.text: A factor that earns the mechanism role is a factor whose interpretation has survived tests like this one.
Above the latent mechanism, the path divides.

On the first route, which stays with the visual system in general, a latent mechanism becomes an established mechanism when its interpretation converges with independent evidence: physiology, anatomy, computational models, and, where it exists, ground truth. This route does not require individual-level precision: a mechanism can be established even when no single observer's score on it is reliable enough to serve as a phenotype.
The second and third routes concern individuals.

text.text: I extend the term to vision, with one change of emphasis.
A latent mechanism is a claim about the visual system in general.
A computational phenotype is a claim about individuals: an observer's stable position on a validated mechanism, measured precisely enough to characterize that person (Peterzell, 2026f).

text.text: To earn the role, a factor needs reliability across sessions, replication across samples, and validity against independent measures.
In return, it lets each observer be described by a profile of factor scores rather than by a single threshold.
The parameters of sequentialsampling decision models, fitted to each observer, are a ready example in vision.
The decision stage is a source of individual differences of its own, distinct from the sensory mechanisms that supply its evidence.

Its parameters are trait-like: drift rate and boundary separation keep high rank-order stability over two years, with correlations of .64 or higher for drift rate and .83 or higher for boundary separation (von Krause et al., 2021), and over a week (Lerche & Voss, 2017), and drift rate covaries with ability across tasks (Ratcliff, Thapar, & McKoon, 2010).

Whether decision parameters form one factor or several, and whether those factors are tuned to the stimulus or domain-general, is a question for the covariance logic of this paper (Section 4.3).
Above the computational phenotype, the individual route branches again.
On the genetic route, a phenotype becomes a heritable phenotype when twin, family, or genomic studies show that a substantial part of its variance is genetic.

Examples include face recognition ability (Wilmer et al., 2010; Zhu et al., 2010) and individual variation in personal color space (Bimler & Kirkland, 2004; see also Paramei, Bimler, & Mislavskaia, 2004).

text.text: Face recognition shows how one factor can earn several roles.

Wilmer and colleagues set out criteria for a specific ability: it should be consistent with theory, measured reliably, show convergent and discriminant validity, have norms, and allow precise individual scores (Wilmer et al., 2012; Wilmer, Germine, & Nakayama, 2014).

text.text: Face recognition meets these criteria.

Two points follow.
Wilmer's criteria for a specific ability correspond closely to the evidence that earns the computational-phenotype rung.

And specific abilities and low-level mechanisms are the same idea at different grains: a high-level ability such as face recognition and a low-level mechanism such as a spatial-frequency channel are both narrow, separable sources of variation, judged by the same evidence.

text.text: What matters is that each role is a separate claim with its own evidence.
A mechanism established for vision in general says nothing yet about any one observer, a heritable phenotype is not yet an endophenotype, and a correlate is not yet a validated marker.
Keeping the roles apart protects the paradigm against its most common failure, overclaiming, and lets each study state plainly which roles its factors have earned and which remain open.
Every experiment with more than one observer already contains a second experiment that is rarely analyzed: the experiment that nature ran on the observers before they arrived.

text.text: Group means show what the average observer can do; covariance shows how the work is divided.

It counts the mechanisms that underlie a function, maps the range and coordinate frame of each, and separates stages such as optics, photoreceptors, and cortex, non-invasively and often from existing data.
Once the factors are known, a single well-chosen stimulus can measure each one, turning a long test into a short one and a threshold into a profile (Section 3.5.3).

The paradigm has developed methods of its own: confirmatory models that adjudicate between competing architectures (Emery et al., 2023); nonmetric multidimensional scaling for structure that is non-linear (Kaneko et al., 2025); Monte Carlo simulation and resampling, which test whether a hypothesized model reproduces the observed correlations and how many observers a structure requires (Emery et al., 2017a; Peterzell, 2026h; Peterzell, Werner, & Kaplan, 1993 , 1995); a formal test of whether loadings are tuned (Peterzell, Enongue, et al., 2026; Peterzell & Serrano-Pedraza, 2026); populations of artificial observers with known answers (Peterzell, in press-a); and intuitive factor analysis, which often shows the structure before any statistic is computed (Peterzell, 2016, in press-b).

The correlations between factors are themselves findings, perhaps the paradigm's most underused payoff.

An experiment on the mean can show that two tasks respond to the same manipulation; only covariance among observers can show whether they share a source of variation in people, and it can do so for any pair of measures taken in the same observers.

Within a single domain, two orientation-tuned contrast factors correlate at about .67, so orientation mechanisms are partly shared rather than independent (Peterzell, Bachtoula, et al., 2026), and optical and neural factors are correlated, so observers with poorer optics also have lower neural sensitivity even after optical correction (Peterzell & Elliott, 2026).

text.text: Perhaps the most important thing individual differences can do for vision science as a whole is to test its constructs.

The field names constructs, such as global processing, magnocellular function, illusion susceptibility, and visual ability, and measures each with a favored task, assuming that different tasks for the same construct measure the same thing.

That is a claim about construct validity in Cronbach and Meehl's (1955) sense, and it can be tested only across individuals: if two tasks measure the same construct, observers who do well on one should do well on the other.

Knowing which visual talents are separate tells us how vision is divided at the level of whole abilities, not just early mechanisms.

Individual differences show which mechanisms change, when, and why, and they separate changes in the eye's optics from changes in the brain.

text.text: In infants, chromatic and luminance factors are coupled; in adults, they are independent.

That coupling means early chromatic and luminance development cannot be treated as independent, which limits what late-sighted patients can tell us about the role of early color experience (Peterzell, 2026b; Peterzell, 2026i).

text.text: In aging, chromatic discrimination declines after about 60, most steeply on the blue-yellow axis (Paramei & Oakley, 2014), while color appearance is largely preserved by recalibration (Section 3.2.3).

text.text: An apparent reorganization of spatial channels in older adults (Min & Reynaud, 2026) may be partly optical rather than neural, because the high-spatial-frequency factor in uncorrected viewing reflects optics (Peterzell, 2026e).

text.text: Within a person, state variables such as sleep, light history, circadian phase, and practice change performance. Mollon et al. (2017) treated these as contamination that masks "true" individual differences.

text.text: That was wrong (Section 4.1): the mechanisms that vary from hour to hour, month to month, and year to year are themselves worth mapping.

What it buys: a lifespan map of how visual mechanisms differentiate and decline, a way to tell optical changes, which can often be corrected, from neural ones, and a framework for studying change within a person.
In plain terms: visual disorders and conditions that affect vision rarely knock out a single mechanism.
Individual differences let us describe each patient by a profile across mechanisms, and let us check whether supposedly related tests measure the same thing.
Color vision deficiency is a continuum, not a category: anomalous trichromats range from near-normal to near-dichromatic.
Some visual measures behave as candidate endophenotypes for psychiatric conditions, such as visual backward masking in schizophrenia (Chkonia et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Some visual measures behave as candidate endophenotypes for psychiatric conditions, such as visual backward masking in schizophrenia <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Chkonia et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Individual differences can also correct a field's assumptions, as when supposed tests of "magnocellular function" turned out to measure different things (Goodbourn et al., 2012; Section 3.1.4).
text.formatted: Individual differences can also correct a field's assumptions, as when supposed tests of "magnocellular function" turned out to measure different things <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Goodbourn et al., 2012</ref>; Section 3.1.4).

text.text: And some differences are differences of kind rather than degree.

Deficiency is not only loss: dichromats detect color-camouflaged targets that trichromats miss (Morgan, Adam, & Mollon, 1992), multidimensional scaling reveals a color dimension that only deuteranomalous observers perceive (Bosten, Robinson, Jordan, & Mollon, 2005), and one carrier of anomalous trichromacy behaved as a tetrachromat on every test (Jordan, Deeb, Bosten, & Mollon, 2010).

text.text: Women with genes for more than three photopigments also report seeing more distinct colors in a spectrum than trichromatic controls do (Jameson, Highnote, & Wasserman, 2001), although reports are a weaker test of four-dimensional color vision than discrimination.
text.formatted: Women with genes for more than three photopigments also report seeing more distinct colors in a spectrum than trichromatic controls do <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Jameson, Highnote, & Wasserman, 2001)</ref>, although reports are a weaker test of four-dimensional color vision than discrimination.

text.text: Observers with poor chromatic discrimination show no chromatic tuning of numerosity adaptation at all (Peterzell, Arrighi, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Observers with poor chromatic discrimination show no chromatic tuning of numerosity adaptation at all <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">(Peterzell, Arrighi, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When groups differ in their factor structure, that difference is itself a finding.
What it buys: diagnostic profiles in place of single numbers, earlier detection through departures from normal structure, and tests that have been checked to measure what they claim.
In plain terms: we can now build many slightly different artificial visual systems and ask whether they differ from each other the way people do.
If they do, we can find out why, by changing one thing at a time, which is impossible with people.

Deep networks that differ only in their random starting weights develop different internal representations, so a trained network is one sample from a population of possible observers (Mehrer et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Deep networks that differ only in their random starting weights develop different internal representations, so a trained network is one sample from a population of possible observers <ref type="bibr" target="#b118">(Mehrer et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Peterzell (in press-a) proposed a computational psychometrics of vision: build a designed population of artificial observers varying in architecture, initialization, training diet, optics, and cone sampling; give them the tests given to humans; and ask whether factor analysis recovers the human factor structure.
A model that reproduces the average human but not the human covariance structure has not explained human vision.
Safeguards keep the benchmark from becoming a target: analytic decisions fixed in advance, a held-out battery, and transfer to domains the model was not tuned on.
What it buys: a new and demanding benchmark for models of vision, and causal tests of where individual differences come from.
In plain terms: sensory mechanisms do not stop at perception.
Individual differences show where visual mechanisms shape counting, naming, and emotional responses, and where they do not.
Numerosity is a clear case.

Correlations among observers in reproducing numbers by action fall off with numerical distance, and factor analysis finds two tuned number channels, one for lower and one for higher numbers (Anobile, Petrizzo, Paiardini, Burr, & Cicchini, 2024).
text.formatted: Correlations among observers in reproducing numbers by action fall off with numerical distance, and factor analysis finds two tuned number channels, one for lower and one for higher numbers <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Anobile, Petrizzo, Paiardini, Burr, & Cicchini, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Numerosity adaptation is selective for salient features (Grasso, Anobile, Arrighi, Burr, & Cicchini, 2022), including color, a selectivity that depends on the automatic categorization of colored information (Grasso, Anobile, Gurioli, Cicchini, & Arrighi, 2025), and its chromatic tuning is narrow and differs across observers (Peterzell, Arrighi, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Numerosity adaptation is selective for salient features <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(Grasso, Anobile, Arrighi, Burr, & Cicchini, 2022)</ref>, including color, a selectivity that depends on the automatic categorization of colored information <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Grasso, Anobile, Gurioli, Cicchini, & Arrighi, 2025)</ref>, and its chromatic tuning is narrow and differs across observers <ref type="bibr" target="#b156">(Peterzell, Arrighi, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Individual differences in hue scaling can supply a realistic perceptual space for models of color naming (Peterzell, 2026c).
text.formatted: Individual differences in hue scaling can supply a realistic perceptual space for models of color naming <ref type="bibr" target="#b146">(Peterzell, 2026c)</ref>.

text.text: Differences in color perception also bear on clinical assessment: color responses to the Rorschach inkblots depend on how each person sees color, a factor the standard scoring systems do not consider (Peterzell, 2026g).
text.formatted: Differences in color perception also bear on clinical assessment: color responses to the Rorschach inkblots depend on how each person sees color, a factor the standard scoring systems do not consider <ref type="bibr">(Peterzell, 2026g)</ref>.

text.text: And separate motion mechanisms predict separate phases of smooth pursuit, linking perception to action (Section 3.1.3).
What it buys: bridges from sensory mechanisms to cognition, language, emotion, and action, and checks on claims that a higher-level effect is "really" sensory, or not.

In plain terms: knowing how people differ tells us who will do well at a task and who will struggle, how to design displays, signals, lighting, and environments for everyone rather than for an average observer who does not exist, and how to fit a device to each user.

The oldest use of individual differences in vision is selection: color vision tests for railway workers followed the Lagerlunda collision of 1875 (Mollon & Cavonius, 2012), and face recognition tests now help select super-recognizers (Russell et al., 2009).

text.text: Whether a vision test predicts performance depends on the task: among ship watchkeepers searching for life rafts, color vision and low-contrast acuity scores predicted daytime detection but not detection through night vision goggles, which remove color (Donderi, 1994).
text.formatted: Whether a vision test predicts performance depends on the task: among ship watchkeepers searching for life rafts, color vision and low-contrast acuity scores predicted daytime detection but not detection through night vision goggles, which remove color <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Donderi, 1994)</ref>.

text.text: Factor analysis can also streamline selection itself: in an occupational vision-screening battery given to Air Force personnel and civilians, it identified a small number of independent dimensions, so that redundant tests could be dropped and operationally relevant ones kept (Seemiller et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Factor analysis can also streamline selection itself: in an occupational vision-screening battery given to Air Force personnel and civilians, it identified a small number of independent dimensions, so that redundant tests could be dropped and operationally relevant ones kept <ref type="bibr" target="#b189">(Seemiller et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The larger use is in design standards, most of which are written for a standard observer: colorimetry rests on standard color matching functions, photometry on a single luminous efficiency function, and accessibility guidelines set contrast ratios computed from luminance alone (World Wide Web Consortium, 2018).

text.text: Anthropometry learned long ago to design cockpits for a range of body sizes; vision has been slower.
The covariance paradigm supplies what better guidelines need.
First, it shows how many independent dimensions a guideline must cover.

A standard based on one measure, such as acuity, implicitly assumes one factor; where there are several, as for contrast sensitivity and stereopsis, a single criterion passes people it should flag and flags people it should pass, and a stereoscopic headset comfortable for one profile of mechanisms may fail for another.
Second, it shows which limitations travel together.
Aging changes several factors, but not in lockstep (Garobbio et al., 2023; Shaqiri et al., 2019), so a single correction for "older users" fits few of them.
text.formatted: Aging changes several factors, but not in lockstep <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Garobbio et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b193">Shaqiri et al., 2019)</ref>, so a single correction for "older users" fits few of them.

text.text: Third, it supplies the parameters for designing to a distribution.

Colorimetry has begun to do this: the CIE physiological observer makes color matching functions depend on age and field size (CIE, 2006), and an individual colorimetric observer model generates populations of observers from the sources of variation that factor analysis of archival color matches first separated (Asano, Fairchild, & Blondé, 2016; MacLeod & Webster, 1983 , 1988).
text.formatted: Colorimetry has begun to do this: the CIE physiological observer makes color matching functions depend on age and field size <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(CIE, 2006)</ref>, and an individual colorimetric observer model generates populations of observers from the sources of variation that factor analysis of archival color matches first separated <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Asano, Fairchild, & Blondé, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b109">MacLeod & Webster, 1983</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b228">, 1988)</ref>.

text.text: The question for design is the one Peterzell (2026d) asked of color, whom a choice helps and whom it hurts, and it applies to every visual dimension a designer can manipulate.
Two design strategies follow.

Universal design serves the whole distribution at once: critical information is carried redundantly, by luminance, shape, or position as well as by color, in palettes that remain distinguishable with color vision deficiency (Peterzell, 2026d).
text.formatted: Universal design serves the whole distribution at once: critical information is carried redundantly, by luminance, shape, or position as well as by color, in palettes that remain distinguishable with color vision deficiency <ref type="bibr" target="#b147">(Peterzell, 2026d)</ref>.

text.text: Individualized design fits the device to the person.
Calibrating a display to the standard observer corrects the device, not the viewer (Asano et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Calibrating a display to the standard observer corrects the device, not the viewer <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Asano et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Displays, headsets, and vehicles can increasingly be tuned to each user, but tuning requires knowing which parameters to set.

Factor structure supplies the answer: the number of independent factors is the number of calibration parameters, and the one-stimulus-per-factor principle (Section 3.5.3) gives the short test that estimates them.
A user's factor profile becomes a calibration profile.
Virtual-reality headsets make the case sharply.

Each embodies one model of its user, with one interpupillary distance, one eye height, one focal distance, and one set of color-matching functions, and an apparent sex difference in cybersickness turned out largely to reflect how well the headset fit each user's interpupillary distance (Stanney, Fidopiastis, & Foster, 2020).

text.text: Driving shows how far the logic reaches.

Driver distraction is usually treated as a single drain on attention, and hands-free laws treat it that way: they remove the manual demand of a call but not the conversation, which degrades simulated driving either way (Strayer & Johnston, 2001).
text.formatted: Driver distraction is usually treated as a single drain on attention, and hands-free laws treat it that way: they remove the manual demand of a call but not the conversation, which degrades simulated driving either way <ref type="bibr" target="#b201">(Strayer & Johnston, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Part of the cost is perceptual: moving gaze off the forward road slowed brake-light detection by roughly 450 ms, whereas cognitive load added little (Wolfe, Sawyer, Kosovicheva, Reimer, & Rosenholtz, 2019).
text.formatted: Part of the cost is perceptual: moving gaze off the forward road slowed brake-light detection by roughly 450 ms, whereas cognitive load added little <ref type="bibr" target="#b235">(Wolfe, Sawyer, Kosovicheva, Reimer, & Rosenholtz, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Treated instead as a multidimensional, person-dependent event, distraction has latent sensory, attentional, imaginal, and affective-autonomic dimensions that covariance could recover from naturalistic driving data, together with the individual differences that predict who is most vulnerable (Peterzell & Service, 2026).

text.text: The link to vision is old. Owsley, Sekuler, and Siemsen (1983) measured contrast sensitivity across adulthood, Sekuler et al. (1984) modeled the structure of individual differences in spatial vision, and Owsley went on to show that the useful field of view predicts crash risk in older drivers (Owsley et al., 1998), although the field it measures is graded rather than divided into useful and useless regions (Wolfe, Dobres, Rosenholtz, & Reimer, 2017); a few supertaskers show little cost from dualtasking (Watson & Strayer, 2010).

text.text: Drivers also differ in how much they need to see.

Younger drivers detected hazards in road video after about 220 ms and chose an evasive steer after about 390 ms, older drivers after about 400 and 600 ms (Wolfe, Seppelt, Mehler, Reimer, & Rosenholtz, 2020), and the age gap replicated online, with wide variation within each age group (Guidi, Kosovicheva, & Wolfe, 2024).
text.formatted: Younger drivers detected hazards in road video after about 220 ms and chose an evasive steer after about 390 ms, older drivers after about 400 and 600 ms <ref type="bibr" target="#b236">(Wolfe, Seppelt, Mehler, Reimer, & Rosenholtz, 2020)</ref>, and the age gap replicated online, with wide variation within each age group <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Guidi, Kosovicheva, & Wolfe, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Naturalistic driving research is now seeking drivingbased markers of Alzheimer disease and other disorders: GPS driving features distinguish older adults with preclinical Alzheimer disease (Bayat et al., 2021), and passive in-vehicle sensors are being developed into digital markers (Babulal et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Naturalistic driving research is now seeking drivingbased markers of Alzheimer disease and other disorders: GPS driving features distinguish older adults with preclinical Alzheimer disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bayat et al., 2021)</ref>, and passive in-vehicle sensors are being developed into digital markers <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Babulal et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: These analyses have used classifiers and regression on many driving features, not the covariance among them.

A covariance analysis would ask how many independent dimensions of driving behavior there are and which carries the disease signal, and would then choose the measure that isolates it: a factor-targeted marker for the road.
It has yet to be done, and it could improve both the assessment of drivers and the design of vehicles and driver-monitoring systems.

Shared, annotated road videos already support repeated laboratory measures of hazard perception (Song, Kosovicheva, & Wolfe, 2023), and the same drivers tested on several such tasks would supply the data it needs.
text.formatted: Shared, annotated road videos already support repeated laboratory measures of hazard perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b195">(Song, Kosovicheva, & Wolfe, 2023)</ref>, and the same drivers tested on several such tasks would supply the data it needs.

text.text: Guidelines built on the average driver protect the average driver.

What it buys: evidence-based selection and occupational standards, guidelines that cover the right number of visual dimensions, designs for the range of real observers rather than the standard observer, and devices calibrated to each user's factor profile.
In plain terms: if we know how many mechanisms underlie a visual function, we know how many measurements we need, and which ones.
That makes tests shorter, cleaner, and easier to interpret.

The one-stimulus-per-factor principle has two phases (Peterzell, in press-b): discovery, in which a function is sampled densely enough to resolve every factor, and assessment, in which one stimulus is placed where each factor loads highest and the others load near zero.

text.text: The savings can be large.
Two orientations can replace ten for contrast sensitivity (Peterzell, Bachtoula, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Two orientations can replace ten for contrast sensitivity <ref type="bibr" target="#b157">(Peterzell, Bachtoula, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For stereopsis, a few spatial frequencies, two orientations, and two temporal frequencies capture the known mechanisms, whereas a standard clinical stereotest samples one point and can miss whole mechanisms.
Each targeted measure becomes a candidate marker for one mechanism (Section 2.5), and an observer's set of marker scores becomes a computational-phenotype profile (Peterzell, 2026f).
text.formatted: Each targeted measure becomes a candidate marker for one mechanism (Section 2.5), and an observer's set of marker scores becomes a computational-phenotype profile <ref type="bibr" target="#b149">(Peterzell, 2026f)</ref>.

text.text: Treatment can then be aimed at a specific mechanism and checked against it, as adaptive optics does when it removes the optical factor and reveals the neural factors it had masked (Peterzell & Elliott, 2026). Thurstone (1950) made the clinical case three quarters of a century ago: two patients with the same audiometric hearing loss can differ markedly in understanding conversation because they differ in auditory closure (Karlin, 1942 , as described by Thurstone, 1950).

text.text: What it buys: shorter tests, cleaner markers, individual profiles in place of single numbers, and treatments that can be aimed at and verified against a specific mechanism.
Nearly a decade ago, Mollon et al. (2017) handed down rules.
text.formatted: Nearly a decade ago, <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Mollon et al. (2017)</ref> handed down rules.

text.text: This section hands them back.
What follows is not a refinement of the 2017 recommendations but a repudiation of them.
They were offered as the one right way, and there is no one right way.
Several of the 2017 warnings remain useful, and I return to them at the end of this section (Section 4.11).
But the central recommendations share a flaw: each treats one design choice as the safe one, when every choice in this field trades one error for another.
The right standard is not a single correct design.

It is a study whose conclusions survive the plausible alternatives, shown by replication, by converging methods, and by reporting how results change when reasonable analytic choices change (Steegen, Tuerlinckx, Gelman, & Vanpaemel, 2016).
text.formatted: It is a study whose conclusions survive the plausible alternatives, shown by replication, by converging methods, and by reporting how results change when reasonable analytic choices change <ref type="bibr" target="#b198">(Steegen, Tuerlinckx, Gelman, & Vanpaemel, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Of all the claims in Mollon et al. (2017), the most consequential, and the most wrong, was the definition on which their methods rested.
text.formatted: Of all the claims in <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Mollon et al. (2017)</ref>, the most consequential, and the most wrong, was the definition on which their methods rested.

text.text: They divided the variance between observers tested on a single occasion into four sources: "constitutional, or other long-term, betweenindividual, variation"; "within-individual variation"; instrumental variation; and variation in the experimenter.
They then stated that the last three "mask the size of any true individual differences."

In that scheme, only stable, long-term differences count as true individual differences, and every way in which a person changes is placed in the same bin as a drifting photometer and a tired experimenter.
The test-retest requirement discussed below rests on that definition.
The definition is not a harmless convention.
It is wrong, and it came from left field.
There are, fittingly, individual differences in how researchers define individual differences.

But that distribution has a center, and the 2017 definition lies many standard deviations away from it. Cronbach's (1957) correlational discipline studies whatever variation nature has imposed on people, not only the variation that holds still.
text.formatted: But that distribution has a center, and the 2017 definition lies many standard deviations away from it. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Cronbach's (1957)</ref> correlational discipline studies whatever variation nature has imposed on people, not only the variation that holds still.

text.text: Changes in a person's vision over hours, days, months, and years are human variability, and they contribute to the differences measured between people on any given day.
Lumping them with instrument error confuses a property of the observer with a property of the apparatus.

There are circadian rhythms in visual function and retinal physiology, including the daily shedding of photoreceptor outer segments (LaVail, 1976); renewal cycles in the tissues of the eye over days, months, and years, with the cumulative effects of light across the lifespan (Werner, Peterzell, & Scheetz, 1990); monthly menstrual cycles, with accompanying changes in sensory function (Farage, Osborn, & MacLean, 2008); seasons, whose changing colors shift color perception (Welbourne et al., 2015); and sleep, light history, adaptation, practice, and learning. Mollon et al. (2017) cited several of these effects themselves, but only as threats to measurement.

text.text: Every one of them is a legitimate object of study.

Variation that is not permanently stable has been factor-analyzed for nearly 80 years, and it contains meaningful, interpretable factors. Cattell, Cattell, and Rhymer (1947) introduced P-technique, factoring the correlations among many measures taken from one person across many days, and recovered definite psychological and physiological factors. Zevon and Tellegen (1982) applied P-technique to daily mood ratings over 90 days and found Positive and Negative Affect within individuals, not only between them.

text.text: Latent state-trait theory treats state variance as reliable, true-score variance to be estimated, not as error to be removed (Steyer, Schmitt, & Eid, 1999).

text.text: Each of these discoveries would have been impossible under a definition that discards variation because it does not hold still.
Vision has documented the same kinds of variation but rarely analyzed them this way.
The timing of the cone-driven electroretinogram changes with the daily light cycle (Hankins, Jones, Jenkins, & Morland, 2001).

text.formatted: Perceptual biases for ambiguous stimuli differ between observers and also drift from day to day within them <ref type="bibr" target="#b221">(Wexler, Duyck, & Mamassian, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: These are individual differences in cycles, and differences in who cycles at all.
Within-person factor analyses of such variation, such as daily contrast sensitivity functions measured across circadian, monthly, and seasonal cycles, appear not yet to have been done in vision.
They are an open opportunity, and exactly the studies the The case for a paradigm shift 32 2017 definition would have ruled out.
Throwing such data away is not caution.
It is discarding the evidence.
None of this denies the value of stability where stability is the point: a computational phenotype or a clinical marker must be stable enough for its purpose (Section 2).
But that is a requirement for particular roles, not a definition of the field.

The cost of a single-right-way approach is easiest to see in the paradigm's own landmarks. MacLeod and Webster (1983, 1988; Webster & MacLeod, 1988) factor-analyzed the color matches that Stiles and Burch (1959) had collected three decades earlier, in another laboratory, to define a standard colorimetric observer.

text.text: Those data were not collected with repeated sessions, a design chosen to protect a factor analysis, or an independent trait against which to validate the factors.
By the standard Mollon et al. (2017) set for demonstrating true individual differences, the reanalysis would not have been undertaken.

text.text: Yet it recovered the separate pigment factors described in Section 1.3, produced direct estimates of the cone absorption spectra, and was cited by Mollon et al. (2017) themselves as an exemplary confirmatory analysis.

text.text: That is not a matter of interpretation: applied as written, the standard excludes one of the paradigm's defining results, and a rule that rules out the field's own best exemplar is wrong.

The same holds across the paradigm's history. Peterzell, Werner, and Kaplan (1993) found interpretable structure in published data from six to eight infants per age group (Banks & Salapatek, 1981), and my reanalysis of Thurstone's (1944) battery recovered separate illusion, switching, and closure factors (Peterzell, 2020). Elliott et al. (2009) designed their adaptiveoptics study to examine optical aberrations in aging, not individual differences, yet its reanalysis separated optical from neural factors (Peterzell & Elliott, 2026). Mollon et al. (2017) conceded the point in their conclusion: "few studies meet all of the requirements of the best practices advocated, though many have yielded plausible and compelling accounts."

text.text: That concession is the right lesson, and it should have been the rule rather than the exception.

Data that fall short of an ideal design can still answer questions, provided the analysis is honest about what the data can and cannot show, deals openly with unruly observations rather than hiding or discarding them (McClelland, 2000), and the result is tested by replication or by converging evidence.
text.formatted: Data that fall short of an ideal design can still answer questions, provided the analysis is honest about what the data can and cannot show, deals openly with unruly observations rather than hiding or discarding them <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">(McClelland, 2000)</ref>, and the result is tested by replication or by converging evidence.

text.text: Discouraging such analyses does not protect the field from error.

It leaves discoveries in the archive, and archives do not last: data sit on obsolete disks and failing drives, in files no current software can read, and in the offices of researchers who retire or die, and then they are lost for good, along with every discovery they still held.

Some of my own data are already gone: the raw data from our study of infant visual evoked potentials for color and luminance are lost, and the results survive only in a conference abstract (Peterzell, Kelly, et al., 1996) and in the supplementary materials of a later commentary (Peterzell, 2026b).

text.text: Datasets that report individual observers should be analyzed for their covariance while they can be, and deposited in public repositories so that others can analyze them later.

Most of the 2017 warnings concern artifacts that vary between observers but have nothing to do with the mechanism under study: fatigue, motivation, mood, distraction, response bias, and the drift of instruments and experimenters.
The concern is real, but these artifacts share a property that Mollon et al. (2017) did not exploit.
text.formatted: The concern is real, but these artifacts share a property that <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Mollon et al. (2017)</ref> did not exploit.

text.text: They act on an observer's performance across the board.
An observer who slept badly, or who adopts a conservative criterion, performs worse across conditions, not only at spatial frequencies between 1 and 2 cycles per degree.
Global artifacts therefore produce a general factor, a positive correlation among all measures.
They do not produce narrowly tuned factors with dips in correlation between neighboring conditions.

This is arithmetic, not opinion: a source of variation that acts equally across conditions adds the same amount to every covariance, and so cannot by itself create correlations that are high within one range of a stimulus dimension and low between ranges.
An artifact that acts unequally across conditions predicts structure that follows its own profile, such as the order of testing, and that prediction can be tested.

The argument is not new. Peterzell, Werner, and Kaplan (1993) set out three possible causes of individual differences in contrast sensitivity and the correlational structure each predicts: measurement error predicts uncorrelated structure, an overall maturational or attentional level predicts equicorrelational structure, and spatial-frequency-tuned mechanisms predict correlations that are high between neighboring frequencies and fall off with distance.
text.formatted: The argument is not new. <ref type="bibr" target="#b175">Peterzell, Werner, and Kaplan (1993)</ref> set out three possible causes of individual differences in contrast sensitivity and the correlational structure each predicts: measurement error predicts uncorrelated structure, an overall maturational or attentional level predicts equicorrelational structure, and spatial-frequency-tuned mechanisms predict correlations that are high between neighboring frequencies and fall off with distance.

text.text: A study that finds only a general factor has good reason to worry about artifacts.

A study that finds several factors, each confined to a contiguous range of the stimulus dimension, has found structure that global artifacts cannot easily produce, and that structure is itself evidence that the variation comes from the mechanisms.
Many of the 2017 safeguards were designed for a threat that tuned factors already argue against.

Whether a factor is tuned can now be tested formally rather than judged by eye (Section 4.10). Mollon et al. (2017) made test-retest reliability across "well-separated occasions" the "minimal requirement" for demonstrating true individual differences, and dismissed reliability from a single session as "seldom a secure argument."

(2017)</ref> made test-retest reliability across "well-separated occasions" the "minimal requirement" for demonstrating true individual differences, and dismissed reliability from a single session as "seldom a secure argument."

text.text: As a requirement, that standard is wrong, and not by a matter of degree.
Test-retest reliability across sessions is valuable when it is available.
It is not the only evidence, and in many studies it is not the strongest.
The requirement also inherits the error of the definition behind it (Section 4.1).

When a person's vision genuinely changes between sessions, a modest test-retest correlation may reflect that change rather than measurement error, and telling the two apart requires reliability within a session, the very evidence the 2017 paper dismissed.
At least four other kinds of evidence show that individual differences are real.
The first is replication of the factor structure in independent samples, which is far harder to obtain by accident than a single test-retest correlation (Peterzell, 2024).
text.formatted: The first is replication of the factor structure in independent samples, which is far harder to obtain by accident than a single test-retest correlation <ref type="bibr">(Peterzell, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The second is recovery of a known ground truth, such as photopigment spectra in engineered mice (Peterzell, 2026h).
text.formatted: The second is recovery of a known ground truth, such as photopigment spectra in engineered mice <ref type="bibr" target="#b151">(Peterzell, 2026h)</ref>.

text.text: The third is tuned structure, for the reasons just given.

The fourth is split-half reliability with correction for attenuation, which Wilmer (2008) recommended and which is adequate when the question is whether a dissociation can be explained by measurement error.
text.formatted: The fourth is split-half reliability with correction for attenuation, which <ref type="bibr" target="#b222">Wilmer (2008)</ref> recommended and which is adequate when the question is whether a dissociation can be explained by measurement error.

text.text: Replication, ground truth, and tuned structure show that the structure is real; whether individual factor scores are precise enough to characterize one observer is a separate question, answered by the reliability of the scores themselves (Section 2.4).
What matters is reliability of differences between people, which a task optimized for differences between conditions may lack (Hedge et al., 2018).
text.formatted: What matters is reliability of differences between people, which a task optimized for differences between conditions may lack <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">(Hedge et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Researchers should report whatever reliability evidence they have, and say which kind it is.
Mollon et al. (2017) recommended Spearman's rank-order correlation "as an alternative, or in addition" to Pearson's, because ranks resist the leverage of outliers.
As a general rule, this is not a point for debate.
It is wrong.

When the data are approximately normally distributed, when outliers have been checked and dealt with, and when there are no ceiling or floor effects that restrict the range, there is no reason to give up the metric.
Converting such data to ranks throws away information that was paid for in observer hours, sacrificing power and precision for nothing in return.
Those conditions are not exotic: psychophysical thresholds are measured on meaningful metric scales, and on a logarithmic scale they are usually close to normally distributed.
For factor analysis, the cost is larger.
Ranking attenuates correlations and produces a matrix of rank correlations that is a non-standard input to factor analysis, so the loadings that come out are harder to read as tuning functions.
Looking at variability in two or three observers is not a crime, as I argue below.
Discarding good metric data is closer to one.
Outliers are a real problem, but the remedy is due diligence, not a blanket transform.

Judd and McClelland's model-comparison approach remains the best practical guide (Correll, Folberg, Judd, McClelland, & Ryan, 2026; Judd & McClelland, 1989; Judd, McClelland, & Ryan, 2017; McClelland, 2000).
text.formatted: Judd and McClelland's model-comparison approach remains the best practical guide <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Correll, Folberg, Judd, McClelland, & Ryan, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Judd & McClelland, 1989;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Judd, McClelland, & Ryan, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">McClelland, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Plot the distributions and the scatterplot matrix, check for ceiling and floor effects, identify outliers with diagnostics designed for the purpose, ask whether each one reflects an error or a genuine observer, treat it accordingly, use robust covariance estimates or the bootstrap where needed, and report whether results change.
When the data genuinely fail these conditions, being non-normal, range-restricted, non-metric, or non-linear, the right tool is a transformation or method chosen for that failure.
Analyzing ranks is itself a transformation, and a crude one, because it discards the spacing between observations.

A transformation chosen to make the distribution approximately normal and the variance homogeneous, such as a logarithmic or other power transformation, usually solves the same problem while keeping the information (Correll et al., 2026; Judd et al., 2017; McClelland, 2000).
text.formatted: A transformation chosen to make the distribution approximately normal and the variance homogeneous, such as a logarithmic or other power transformation, usually solves the same problem while keeping the information <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Correll et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Judd et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b116">McClelland, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Psychophysicists already do this with log thresholds.
Where no transformation suffices, a method designed for the data, such as nonmetric multidimensional scaling, is the next step (Kaneko et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Where no transformation suffices, a method designed for the data, such as nonmetric multidimensional scaling, is the next step <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Kaneko et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Ranks are one tool among these, chosen when the data call for them, not a default applied to everything.

4.6 Order and blocking: preferences, not prerequisites Mollon et al. (2017) argued that tests should often be given in the same fixed order to every participant, so that order-specific strategies and learning do not create spurious individual differences.
text.formatted: 4.6 Order and blocking: preferences, not prerequisites <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Mollon et al. (2017)</ref> argued that tests should often be given in the same fixed order to every participant, so that order-specific strategies and learning do not create spurious individual differences.

text.text: A fixed order replaces a possible artifact with a certain one.
The confound is not a risk that judgment can weigh; the design guarantees it.
Fatigue and practice become part of the measure, and adjacent conditions become artificially correlated.
The 2017 paper acknowledged this and left the choice to "nice judgement."

The better default is to randomize or counterbalance, to record order, and to model it, entering order into the model as a predictor whose contribution can be tested rather than assumed (Correll et al., 2026; Judd et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The better default is to randomize or counterbalance, to record order, and to model it, entering order into the model as a predictor whose contribution can be tested rather than assumed <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Correll et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Judd et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The paper also warned that interleaving conditions can create spurious factors when observers attend selectively to some conditions, and it favored separate blocks.
Here the recommendation itself is reasonable: blocking is often the better design, and its own cost, tying each condition to a time slot, can be reduced by counterbalancing the order of blocks.
What does not follow is that data collected without blocking should be set aside.
A design preference is not a criterion for admissibility.

When conditions were interleaved, the researcher's task is the one that applies to every imperfect dataset: acknowledge the possible artifact, state the alternative hypothesis it implies, and test it against the data.
Selective attention to some conditions predicts a particular pattern, factors that follow whatever an observer could attend to, which can be compared with the tuned structure a mechanism predicts.

Where possible, it can be settled directly by comparing interleaved and blocked designs in the same observers, and a dataset that leaves the alternative open should be reported with that caveat, not discarded.

A design that makes an artifact impossible to detect is worse than one that lets it be measured. Mollon et al. (2017) raised the question of whether corrections for multiple comparisons should account for every behavioral measure in a study, in addition to the genes or voxels being tested.
text.formatted: A design that makes an artifact impossible to detect is worse than one that lets it be measured. <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Mollon et al. (2017)</ref> raised the question of whether corrections for multiple comparisons should account for every behavioral measure in a study, in addition to the genes or voxels being tested.

text.text: For factor-analytic work, blanket correction is the wrong tool, and this is not a question of how conservative one prefers to be.

In the terms of the model-comparison approach, the question is which of several competing models best accounts for the data, how many factors and with what loadings, not how many of many separate tests reach significance (Correll et al., 2026; Judd et al., 2017).
text.formatted: In the terms of the model-comparison approach, the question is which of several competing models best accounts for the data, how many factors and with what loadings, not how many of many separate tests reach significance <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Correll et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">Judd et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The real risk in exploratory work is overfitting, and the defenses against it are replication in new samples, held-out data, factor-retention criteria such as parallel analysis (Horn, 1965), confirmatory tests of structure proposed in advance, and pre-registration of the analyses that matter.
text.formatted: The real risk in exploratory work is overfitting, and the defenses against it are replication in new samples, held-out data, factor-retention criteria such as parallel analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Horn, 1965)</ref>, confirmatory tests of structure proposed in advance, and pre-registration of the analyses that matter.

text.text: A factor model does not test the correlations one at a time, so correcting them one at a time corrects for tests that were never made.

Applying Bonferroni correction to every correlation in a small psychophysical sample mostly buries real structure. Mollon et al. (2017) concluded that "there is currently no solution" to the problem of separating perceptual effects from response biases in individual differences.
text.formatted: Applying Bonferroni correction to every correlation in a small psychophysical sample mostly buries real structure. <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Mollon et al. (2017)</ref> concluded that "there is currently no solution" to the problem of separating perceptual effects from response biases in individual differences.

text.text: That conclusion was wrong.
Signal detection theory has provided ways to separate sensitivity from criterion for more than half a century (Green & Swets, 1966).
text.formatted: Signal detection theory has provided ways to separate sensitivity from criterion for more than half a century <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Green & Swets, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: The forced-choice methods used for most psychophysical thresholds were introduced to make performance largely independent of criterion, but they are not bias-free. Klein (2001) showed that a preference for one interval lowers the d′ computed from pooled percent correct.
text.formatted: The forced-choice methods used for most psychophysical thresholds were introduced to make performance largely independent of criterion, but they are not bias-free. <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">Klein (2001)</ref> showed that a preference for one interval lowers the d′ computed from pooled percent correct.

text.text: The loss grows with the square of the bias, so it is negligible when the bias is small and can inflate a threshold by tens of percent when it is large.

Interval and position biases are common, and they vary in size and sign across observers and can depend on the stimulus conditions (García-Pérez & Alcalá-Quintana, 2011; Jäkel & Wichmann, 2006; Yeshurun, Carrasco, & Maloney, 2008). Mollon et al. (2017) cited Klein for the problem, but Klein also supplied the correction: record responses by interval and average the interval-specific z scores, a correction he was surprised to find "rarely used" (Klein, 2001 (Klein, , p. 1425)).

(2017)</ref> cited Klein for the problem, but Klein also supplied the correction: record responses by interval and average the interval-specific z scores, a correction he was surprised to find "rarely used" <ref type="bibr" target="#b94">(Klein, 2001</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Klein, , p. 1425))</ref>.

text.text: His point is a reason to model bias, not to despair of it.

A bias that acts alike across conditions contributes mainly to a general factor (Section 4.3), but its effect on uncorrected scores depends on where each condition sits on its psychometric function, so it cannot simply be assumed away.

The remedy is to record the interval or location of every trial; to estimate bias and sensitivity jointly, including with models that allow an undecided response or that separate sensory from decisional bias (García-Pérez & Alcalá-Quintana, 2011; Linares, Aguilar-Lleyda, & López-Moliner, 2019); to analyze bias-corrected sensitivity; and to enter the bias estimates in the factor model as variables of their own, which tests directly whether bias rather than sensitivity carries any tuned structure.
text.formatted: The remedy is to record the interval or location of every trial; to estimate bias and sensitivity jointly, including with models that allow an undecided response or that separate sensory from decisional bias <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(García-Pérez & Alcalá-Quintana, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Linares, Aguilar-Lleyda, & López-Moliner, 2019)</ref>; to analyze bias-corrected sensitivity; and to enter the bias estimates in the factor model as variables of their own, which tests directly whether bias rather than sensitivity carries any tuned structure.

text.text: Bias is also an individual difference in its own right, not only an artifact to remove.

Observers hold stable, idiosyncratic criteria that are linked, modestly, to how each encodes the stimulus (Rahnev, 2021), and choice-history biases are idiosyncratic, act on evidence accumulation rather than only on its starting point (Urai, de Gee, Tsetsos, & Donner, 2019), and are stable across sessions two to four weeks apart (Urai & Donner, 2022).
