text.text: A problem that can be measured is not a problem without a solution.
The number of observers a study needs depends on how reliable the measures are, how much observers truly differ, how many factors must be resolved, and how the observers are distributed.
Samples whose observers cluster near the mean estimate relations far less efficiently than samples that span the full range, including the extremes (McClelland & Judd, 1993).
text.formatted: Samples whose observers cluster near the mean estimate relations far less efficiently than samples that span the full range, including the extremes <ref type="bibr" target="#b117">(McClelland & Judd, 1993)</ref>.

text.text: A small sample of observers who differ widely can carry more information than a large sample of observers who are alike.
When signal is high, small samples suffice.
Resampling from 86 mice showed that samples of 10 to 12 reproduced the full-sample correlation structure closely and recovered the expected photopigment factors (Peterzell, 2026h, in press-b).
text.formatted: Resampling from 86 mice showed that samples of 10 to 12 reproduced the full-sample correlation structure closely and recovered the expected photopigment factors <ref type="bibr">(Peterzell, 2026h, in press-b)</ref>.

text.text: The point is old: Peterzell and Teller (1996) recovered the two coarsest spatial channels from seven adults, and Peterzell (2016) showed factor structure visible in the contrast sensitivity functions of three or four observers.
text.formatted: The point is old: <ref type="bibr">Peterzell and Teller (1996)</ref> recovered the two coarsest spatial channels from seven adults, and Peterzell (2016) showed factor structure visible in the contrast sensitivity functions of three or four observers.

text.text: When signal is low, much larger samples are needed.
The right way to set sample size is to simulate it: generate data with the expected structure and reliability, and find the sample at which the structure is recovered.
This matters most for expensive physiology and patient studies, where the 2017 advice would have discouraged feasible work.
The belief that small datasets are useless is one of the most costly in this field, because it stops analyses before they start.
The familiar rules of thumb, such as 100 cases or five to ten per variable, came from questionnaire research, where items are noisy and loadings modest.
Psychophysical thresholds from practiced observers are far more reliable, and their factors load strongly on many measures.

Methodological work shows that the sample a factor analysis needs depends on the size of the loadings and communalities and on how many measures define each factor, not on a fixed number (MacCallum, Widaman, Zhang, & Hong, 1999).
text.formatted: Methodological work shows that the sample a factor analysis needs depends on the size of the loadings and communalities and on how many measures define each factor, not on a fixed number <ref type="bibr" target="#b108">(MacCallum, Widaman, Zhang, & Hong, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: With high loadings, few factors, and many measures, samples well below 50 can recover the structure reliably (de Winter, Dodou, & Wieringa, 2009).
text.formatted: With high loadings, few factors, and many measures, samples well below 50 can recover the structure reliably <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(de Winter, Dodou, & Wieringa, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Many datasets dismissed as too small already contain answers, and should be analyzed with the uncertainty reported honestly.
It is not a crime to look at variability in data from only two or three observers and venture hypotheses.
In fact, it is a very good idea, as history has shown.

Dalton (1798) began the scientific study of color deficiency by describing one observer who differed from others, himself, and König and Dieterici (1886) derived the cone sensitivities from a handful of observers who differed in kind.

Classical psychophysics has long drawn conclusions about mechanisms from a few practiced observers, often the authors themselves, and there is no principled reason to accept inferences from a few observers' means and forbid inferences from their differences.

When the curves of two or three observers differ systematically in one range of a stimulus dimension but not another, that pattern is information, and it is legitimate to plot it and venture a hypothesis about what produced it.
This is intuitive factor analysis (Section 4.10), which Mollon et al. (2017) themselves endorsed as a way to see structure in the data.
text.formatted: This is intuitive factor analysis (Section 4.10), which <ref type="bibr" target="#b123">Mollon et al. (2017)</ref> themselves endorsed as a way to see structure in the data.

text.text: Exploration is not confirmation, and a hypothesis drawn from three observers must be tested in more.
But generating hypotheses is how every paradigm begins, and a rule that forbids looking at small samples forbids discovery at its earliest and cheapest stage.

Factor analysis is the paradigm's workhorse, but it rests on assumptions: approximately linear relations, multivariate normality for maximum-likelihood estimation and its tests, and a rotation that is not unique.
Exploratory factor analysis proposes structure; confirmatory analysis and replication test it.
Deciding how many factors to keep needs the same care.
The usual rules, Kaiser's criterion, the scree test, parallel analysis, and the minimum average partial test, ask how large a factor is.

The MacLeod-Webster criterion asks instead whether a factor's loadings change in an orderly way along the stimulus dimension (MacLeod & Webster, 1983; Webster & MacLeod, 1988), which is the question that matters when mechanisms are expected to be tuned.

text.text: These plots should be published routinely.
Several 2017 recommendations remain sound as best practices.
Cases and controls should be tested interleaved in time and place, not cases first and controls later.
Reliabilities should be reported where they are available, so that effect sizes can be corrected for attenuation and absent correlations can be interpreted.
Genetic association studies should guard against population stratification.
And instruments drift: displays, light sources, and anomaloscopes change with time and temperature, so drift should be controlled or measured where possible.
These recommendations let artifacts be detected or prevented without sacrificing information, which is a useful test to apply to any recommendation in this field.
But they are best practices, not conditions of admission.
A dataset that lacks calibration logs, reliability estimates, or interleaved controls has not thereby lost its value.
It has gained an alternative hypothesis that must be stated and, where possible, tested.

Instrument drift, for example, predicts structure that follows the order or date of testing rather than the stimulus dimension, and a general factor rather than tuned ones, so it can often be checked in the data themselves.
Where it cannot be checked, the caveat belongs in the report and the data belong in the analysis.
The aim of every recommendation in this section is the same: not to rule data out, but to make clear what each dataset can and cannot show.
Section 4 argued each correction at length.
In brief, individual differences include all human variability, not only stable traits, and changes within a person contain interpretable factors (Section 4.1).
Imperfect data are not suspect: they produced the paradigm's landmark results and should be analyzed, with limitations stated, before they are lost (Section 4.2).
Artifacts need not be removed by design alone, because global artifacts produce general factors and tuned structure is evidence against them (Section 4.3).
Test-retest reliability across sessions is not the minimal requirement; replication of structure, ground truth, tuned structure, and withinsession reliability all count (Section 4.4).
Rank statistics are not a default: well-behaved metric data keep their metric, and misbehaving data get diagnosis and a transformation chosen for the failure (Section 4.5).
A fixed test order guarantees a confound; randomization or counterbalancing with order modeled is better, and blocking is a preference, not a condition for using the data (Section 4.6).
A factor model is one model, defended against overfitting by replication, held-out data, and confirmatory tests, not by correcting every measure (Section 4.7).

Response bias has solutions: forced choice is not bias-free, but signal detection, bias-corrected scoring, and joint models of bias and sensitivity address it, and tuned structure argues against a global bias (Section 4.8).

Large samples are not always necessary: the sample depends on reliability, effect size, the spread of observers, and the number of factors, and small samples of practiced observers can recover structure (Section 4.9).
And individual differences are not a resource to be mined with caution, but a paradigm with its own objects, standards, and products (Sections 1-3).
My own earlier work needed correction too.
For decades, I and others read a high-spatialfrequency factor in contrast sensitivity as a neural channel; adaptive optics showed that it was optical (Section 2.2).
That correction came from the paradigm itself, which is how it should work.
The 2017 paper also got important things right.
It assembled the special issue that brought much of this work together.
It recognized that agreement among observers with very different eyes reveals normalization, a finding only individual differences can show.
And several of its practical warnings remain sound (Section 4.11).
The error was not in caring about artifacts.
It was in turning preferences into rules, and rules into reasons not to look.
The twelve pillars of Figure 2 hold up a roof, and the roof is the paradigm's long-term goal: a computational atlas of human visual variation.

text.text: An atlas is not a list of findings but a common map, built to shared standards, that anyone can consult and extend.
The atlas has three layers, one for each route in Figure 1.
text.formatted: The atlas has three layers, one for each route in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">1</ref>.

text.text: The first is a map of mechanisms: for each visual function, how many factors underlie it, how each is tuned and in what coordinate frame, the stage at which it arises, and how strongly it is coupled to the others, together with the decision and confidence parameters observers bring to every task, which are idiosyncratic yet stable over weeks (Navajas et al., 2017) and only partly domain-general (Mazancieux, Fleming, Souchay, & Moulin, 2020).

text.text: The correlations between factors belong in this layer, because they are the connections between mechanisms (Section 3.1.3).

The second layer records where each factor's variation comes from: heritability and genes, development and aging, environment and culture, and the daily, monthly, and seasonal cycles along which it changes within a person.

The third layer records how each factor is best measured and used: the optimal stimulus for it, normative distributions, its value as a marker for disease, and its role as a parameter in calibrating devices to individual users.
Every entry would carry the role it has earned in the sense of Figure 1, and the evidence for it.

text.text: That grading is what keeps an atlas from becoming a catalog of overclaims.
Much of the atlas can be built now, and some of it only now.
Four steps would go most of the way.
First, report the covariance.
Nearly every study in vision tests more than one observer.

Publishing individual data and the correlation matrix alongside the mean costs little beyond preparing the data, and depositing the data in public repositories turns every study into a contribution to the atlas (Section 3.1.5).
Archival data should be recovered and analyzed while they still exist (Section 4.2).
Second, use common reference measures.

A shared battery, designed by the onestimulus-per-factor principle and sampled densely enough during discovery to resolve every factor, would let results from different laboratories, populations, and decades be placed on the same map (Peterzell, in press-b).

text.text: Broad batteries exist (Bosten et al., 2017; Cappe et al., 2014); what is needed is dense sampling within each function, linked across functions in the same observers.

text.text: Third, connect levels and domains.

The atlas is most valuable where it links psychophysics to evoked potentials, imaging, genetics, and the clinic in the same people, and where it links one domain to another, color to luminance, stereopsis to contrast, perception to action and cognition (Section 3.1.3).
These links are where individual differences give answers that no other method can.
Fourth, use artificial observers as a test bed.

Populations of model observers that differ the way people do can test whether a proposed atlas entry reflects a mechanism or an artifact of analysis, and whether a model of vision reproduces the human covariance structure as well as the human mean (Peterzell, in press-a).

text.text: Experiments tell us what the average visual system does and why; the atlas tells us how that system is divided, how its parts vary together, where the variation comes from, and how to measure it in one person.

A theory of spatial vision must explain both the mean contrast sensitivity function and the factors beneath it, and a theory of color both the average hue circle and the many narrowly tuned factors on which observers differ. Cronbach (1957) asked for "combined, not parallel, labors" between the experimental and correlational disciplines.

text.text: In vision science, the correlational discipline has existed for more than a century, but mostly in the shadows, kept alive by a small group.
Nearly a decade ago, Mollon et al. (2017) brought it into the light and then handed it a set of rules that would have kept many of its best results from being found.

text.text: This paper has argued that those rules should be set aside and that the paradigm has earned a place beside the experimental mainstream.
What it offers is broad.
It identifies the mechanisms of vision, optical, retinal, neural, and psychophysical, counts them, and maps their tuning.
It tests whether the field's constructs measure what they claim to.
It traces variation to genes, development, aging, environment, culture, and the cycles of each person's life, and detects genetic variation and its consequences.
It supplies markers that diagnose disease, track its progress, and aim and verify treatment at a specific mechanism.
It holds models of vision, human and artificial, to the standard of reproducing human covariance as well as the human mean.
And it lets displays, devices, and standards be designed for real observers rather than an average one.
Its long-term goal is a shared atlas of human visual variation that brings these together.

To return to the informal title, the good is what the paradigm buys: mechanisms counted and tuned, phenotypes and markers, tests of construct validity, links across domains and levels, and designs that fit real people.
The bad is a set of prescriptions that mistook preferences for requirements.
The ugly is the data already lost because no one looked at the differences while they still could.
The good is within reach, the bad can be corrected, and the ugly can be stopped.
Every experiment with more than one observer already contains a second experiment.
The task now is to analyze it.
